title: Service Star: Abhijay Potluri, 14, Teaches Coding Worldwide
summary:
Abhijay Potluri is only 14, but he's already running a nonprofit and teaching kids around the world. The Boxborough, Massachusetts, teen started Kids Who Teach, which offers lessons in coding, public speaking, and problem-solving to kids in India, Indonesia, Uganda, and the U.S. He's also a former TFK Kid Reporter.

Abhijay's drive to help others started early. "I've always liked knowing how things work," he says. "My brother and I used to play I Spy when we were little. As I got older, I started spotting real problems the same way." During the COVID-19 pandemic, he learned to code and realized kids could build things that help people.

He also helped organize a fundraiser for people affected by a fire near his home. "I was not affected by the fire, but I saw families struggling. Kids in my school became homeless," he says. "What stuck with me was seeing every age show up: fourth graders donating next to adults. It taught me that a small community can make a real difference."

Balancing school, sports, and his projects isn't easy. "School, sports, and my projects all pile up on the same day," he admits. He also faces doubt from people who think kids can't make real change. "People often think kids cannot make real change because we are young," he says. "That gets to me." But he plans out his day and gets things done. "When I plan out my day, I get things done and still have fun," he says.

His proudest achievement is teaching kids in so many different places. "Reaching that many different places is what makes me proudest," he says. His advice to other kids? "The hardest part is figuring out where to start. Once you make a plan or a timeline, it gets a lot easier. You just need to take the first step."

Abhijay's story was shared in an interview with TFK reader Aadhav Bhaskaran. It shows that age doesn't have to limit what you can do.
why_it_matters: Abhijay's story is a test of a bigger question: how much can young people actually change on their own, and what schools, laws and adults would have to do to give more of them the same chance.

background_read: Time for Kids, or TFK (a news magazine for kids published by TIME), selects Kid Reporters — students who interview people and write stories for other kids — and Abhijay was one of them.

Boxborough, Massachusetts (a small town northwest of Boston) is the kind of community where a single event can pull a whole neighborhood together, which is what happened after a fire affected local families.

The COVID-19 pandemic (a worldwide outbreak of a new coronavirus that spread in 2020 and closed schools in many countries) pushed millions of students online, and many of them, like Abhijay, used the time to teach themselves tech skills such as coding.

A nonprofit is an organization that puts its money back into its mission instead of paying profits to owners; in the United States these groups register with the government and are usually overseen by a board, and because minors generally cannot sign legal contracts, kid-run nonprofits almost always need an adult to handle the paperwork.
Many schools encourage or require community service, and student-led projects often start tiny — a few students and a free video call — before spreading to other countries.

perspectives.description: Free lessons in coding and public speaking reach kids in four countries, and the teenagers who teach them gain real experience in leadership and communication. It also shows that a young person can run something structured, not just a one-off school project.

A 14-year-old cannot sign contracts, and a small volunteer effort often depends on one person's free time and internet connection. If Abhijay gets buried in exams, the lessons may simply stop — a risk adult-run organizations are built to survive.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — the tools outran the rules
perspectives.description: This is part of a wider pattern: cheap video calls, free coding platforms and the online shift during the pandemic let teenagers run global projects that once required adults, offices and budgets. The technology changed faster than the legal and school systems around youth-led groups.

The real question is durability. If schools and nonprofits help students like Abhijay with legal structure, funding and mentors, projects such as Kids Who Teach could outlive their founders and become a model for other kids trying to take the first step.
